claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by the degree of lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion promotes sluggish atomic diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion caused by lattice distortion suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions.
A larger spread in constituent atomic radii, or addition of a minor size-mismatched element, will increase lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion produces local lattice strain and a disordered atomic-energy landscape.
The disordered atomic-energy landscape slows atomic diffusion and impedes growth of secondary phases.
Reduced atom mobility maintains high configurational entropy during prolonged thermal stress.
Near-equiatomic multielement solid solutions can retain a single-phase structure at elevated temperature.
Nanoparticles engineered for greater lattice distortion will coarsen less than moderately distorted baseline nanoparticles during thermal aging.
Nanoparticles engineered for greater lattice distortion will exhibit less elemental segregation than baseline nanoparticles during thermal aging.
Nanoparticles engineered for greater lattice distortion will retain a single-phase structure better than baseline nanoparticles during thermal aging.
Baseline nanoparticles made from elements with similar atomic radii are prone to mild phase separation and elemental segregation under the stated service conditions.
The proposed lattice-distortion mechanism applies to single-phase nanoparticles throughout 473–1923 K.
Excessive lattice strain may cause premature mechanical instability.
Severe oxidation may dominate degradation and invalidate the lattice-distortion mechanism.
Failure of the high-distortion particles to show significantly less coarsening, phase separation, or segregation than the control under identical aging conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
